description: O-negative individuals are universal red blood cell donors. Their red cells lack A, B, and Rh antigens, making them vital in trauma and emergency transfusions.
O-positive is one of the most common blood types worldwide. Their red blood cells can be transfused to any Rh-positive patient.
A-negative individuals have A antigens without the Rh factor. They can safely donate red blood cells to both A and AB recipients.
A-positive is a common blood type containing A and Rh antigens. They can receive red blood cells from A and O donors.
B-negative is a rarer blood type containing B antigens without the Rh factor. They can donate red blood cells to B and AB patients.
B-positive contains B antigens and the Rh factor. They can receive red blood cells from B and O types and donate to B+ and AB+ recipients.
AB-negative is the rarest blood group. Because their red cells have both A and B antigens, they can donate red blood cells only to other AB patients.
AB-positive individuals are universal red blood cell recipients because their blood recognizes A, B, and Rh antigens without producing antibodies against them.
